title: A case report reappraising the usefulness of Valsalva manoeuvre in drug-refractory ventricular tachycardia
case_prompt:
A 74-year-old man with a history of remote myocardial infarction presented to the emergency department with dizziness and palpitations. He denied chest pain. One week earlier, he had outpatient Holter monitoring for syncopal palpitations without a diagnosis. On arrival, his heart rate was 180 bpm and blood pressure 102/78 mmHg. Physical examination, including cardiovascular and respiratory systems, was unremarkable.

A 12-lead ECG showed a broad complex tachycardia with features suggestive of ventricular tachycardia. Intravenous adenosine (6 mg, 6 mg, 12 mg) via a large antecubital cannula produced no change in rate, and transient side effects confirmed successful administration. Intravenous amiodarone was started, but the patient’s blood pressure fell to 80/60 mmHg, necessitating synchronized DC cardioversion to sinus rhythm.

Two hours later, telemetry documented a recurrent broad complex tachycardia at similar rate but with a different QRS morphology. While he remained hemodynamically stable, a Valsalva manoeuvre was attempted and immediately terminated the tachycardia. Over the next 12 hours, multiple episodes of this second tachycardia occurred, each consistently terminated by Valsalva manoeuvre. Subsequent routine blood tests, including calcium, magnesium, and potassium, were within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. SVT with aberrancy was considered but ruled out—“lack of tachycardia response with adenosine”  
2. Right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) VT was considered for the first tachycardia given LBBB morphology—“…VT-1 possesses the same ECG morphologies as RVOT VT … yet failed to be terminated by adenosine”  
3. Macro-reentrant scar-related VT was diagnosed for VT-1—“LBBB morphology and inferior axis … localized to anteroseptal exit, corroborated by cardiac MRI findings of scarring”  
4. Purkinje-system VT was diagnosed for VT-2—“RBBB morphology with sharp initial QRS deflection … capture beat … suggests VT arising from the His-Purkinje conducting system”  
5. Electrolyte disturbance was excluded as a cause—“Routine blood tests were normal.”
